Staging environment for tomorrow’s demo

standup.text:
Payments, migration and auth standup

We reviewed progress on the payments retry fix, orders migration, search relevance and auth refactor. Auth rollout remains blocked by staging identity-provider configuration; the search results need more traffic before drawing conclusions.

## Action items
- [ ] Finish the webhook retry dashboard panel by end of tomorrow (me)
- [ ] Investigate whether the new SDK version explains Jen’s feature-flag evaluation latency increase (me)
- [ ] Send Priya the audience configuration notes from the billing service work today (me)
- [ ] Confirm the Kubernetes upgrade date in the channel (me)
- [ ] Finish the orders migration rollback path by Thursday (Tomasz)
- [ ] Paste the platform ticket for the staging identity-provider issue in the channel (Priya)

## My update
- Merged the payments callback webhook retry fix following yesterday’s outage.
  - It previously retried indefinitely on 4xx responses; it now backs off and stops after five retries.
- Estimated the dashboard panel work at half a day to a day.

## Tomasz
- Ran the orders-table migration script against a full staging copy in about 40 minutes, with no observed locks.
- The rollback path is half-written; work was interrupted by the certificate-renewal issue.

## Jen
- Put the new search ranker into shadow mode on Monday.
  - Click-through is up about 0.4%, which Jen considers within noise rather than a confirmed win.
  - Jen wants at least another week of traffic before reporting results to product.
- Shadow traffic through the feature flags shows a possible 8 ms increase in p99 flag-evaluation latency.
  - I suspect the SDK version I upgraded last week may be responsible.

## Priya
- The session-token auth refactor is basically done, with everything moved off the old cookie helper.
- The staging identity provider cannot issue tokens with the new audience claim.
  - This blocks staging verification, which is required for production rollout sign-off.
  - A ticket is open with the platform team, but their workload makes the timing uncertain: possibly today, possibly next week.
  - I encountered a similar issue on the billing service and think the audience may need to be added to the IdP’s allowed list.

## Open questions
- Is the Kubernetes upgrade now scheduled for the twentieth because of the freeze, rather than next week?

hiring.text:
Rahul Venkataraman senior backend debrief

We reviewed Rahul Venkataraman’s four interview rounds and agreed to move forward to reference checks. Strong system design and positive motivation signals were balanced against mixed coding results and an unresolved concern about his role in previous team attrition.

## Decisions
- Move Rahul forward to reference checks.

## Action items
- [ ] Contact the recruiter today to get a reference list with two former managers and one peer (me).
- [ ] Ask references about Rahul’s role in team attrition, how he worked with the team, whether teammates would work with him again, and how he handles losing a technical argument (me).
- [ ] Send the debrief summary after the meeting (me).

## System design — Priya
- Strong hire signal: Rahul proactively asked about write volume and designed an event-store partitioning scheme.
  - Handled rebalance questions well, including backpressure and idempotent consumers.
- Was candid about gaps in production experience.
  - Had not run the particular broker in production and would check failover semantics before committing to it; Priya viewed that positively.
- Team dynamics were not covered in this round.

## First coding round — Dmitri
- Leaning no hire, but not a hard no.
- Solved the interval-merge problem, but spent about ten minutes on an incorrect approach before correcting it.
  - Dmitri appreciated his thinking aloud.
- Did not finish the concurrent cache-eviction problem.
  - Structure and locking were mostly right, but he ran out of time and struggled to explain a race condition.

## Second coding round — Imani
- Lean hire: finished both problems with clean code and wrote tests without prompting.
- Limited clarifying questions on the second problem raised a scoping concern.
  - He handled the relevant edge case, but Imani was unsure whether he would reliably identify such cases.
  - More evidence on how he scopes work would be needed for a strong hire rating.

## Hiring manager chat — Lena
- Positive culture and motivation signals: thoughtful about past work and specific about wanting to leave.
  - His motivation was not money; after two years maintaining a monolith, he wants to build new things.
- Described losing a rewrite disagreement with his previous manager and accepting the outcome.
  - Was honest that he would have pushed harder on one aspect.
- Briefly implied he may have contributed to attrition on his last team, then moved on.
  - Lena did not have time to probe whether this was humility or a substantive concern.
  - Priya considered it worth asking about, but not a dealbreaker.

## Open questions
- How should the conflicting coding results be weighed?
- Did Rahul contribute to previous team attrition, and what does that indicate about his collaboration?

oneonone.text:
Ingestion redesign and growth path

Daniela and I discussed moving toward design ownership and cross-team leadership, with an ingestion redesign proposal as a potential opportunity. We agreed on a proposal deadline and postmortem improvements; ownership of the broader redesign and a path to the staff track remain conditional.

## Decisions
- Start the proposal review with Daniela; she will decide who else sees it.
- Meet again at the same time next week.

## Action items
- [ ] Draft a one-page ingestion redesign proposal with the problem, a couple of options, and a rough estimate by this Friday; Monday is acceptable if I notify Daniela. Write it so Marcus can read it cold, and flag unknowns (me)
- [ ] Give the alerting gap its own section in the postmortem and sharpen the contributing factors (me)
- [ ] Add the outdated rollback runbook to the postmortem as an action item with me as owner, and update it; tentatively aim for the end of next week, with flexibility because it is less urgent than the proposal (me)
- [ ] Ping Joaquin for ingestion cluster throughput metrics; mention that Daniela approved twenty minutes of his time (me)
- [ ] Loop me into the context around Priya’s team’s downstream consumer work and consider potential overlap with the ingestion redesign (Daniela)

## Growth and design ownership
- I feel like I am treading water after roughly eight months of integrations, bug fixes, and occasional migrations.
  - I want to design work, not only implement someone else’s designs, and would like end-to-end ownership of a design doc.
- Daniela saw promise in my retry logic design doc from last spring.
  - Marcus highlighted it in review; Daniela’s view is that I need more scope to build on those instincts.
- Q3 felt like a doable target for greater ownership, with the ingestion redesign floated as a candidate.
  - Daniela cautioned that one version could conflict with Priya’s team’s downstream work; broader ownership was parked pending context.
- The staff track is a possible longer-term path, not a promise.
  - Daniela said successful ingestion work and demonstrated cross-team scope would be meaningful signals, framing this as an opportunity rather than a test.

## Billing rollout and postmortem
- The billing service rollout shipped Tuesday and was mostly smooth.
  - A smaller recurrence of the cache issue was caught in staging, showing the value of the earlier postmortem work.
- Daniela thought the root cause section was good, but the contributing factors needed more emphasis.
  - Alerting did not fire for forty minutes, which she described as the most actionable fact in the document.
  - I had hesitated because the on-call setup is Dev’s area; Daniela emphasized prevention rather than making anyone look good or bad.
- The rollback runbook was out of date and had only been mentioned in a comment.

## Open questions
- How should the ingestion redesign be scoped to avoid conflict with Priya’s team’s downstream consumer work?
- Will I take ownership of the broader redesign, and will it provide the cross-team scope needed for progress toward the staff track?

sales.text:
Harbor Freight Logistics Lintly pilot

We explored Lintly’s fit for Harbor Freight Logistics’ slow code reviews and outlined a six-week platform-team pilot. Security approval, pilot pricing, and the kickoff date remain pending, with SOC 2 Type II requirements the main procurement concern.

## Decisions
- Plan a six-week pilot for roughly 8–10 platform-team developers, with success criteria defined together.
- Run warn-only for at least the first two weeks; security-only blocking may follow.
- Treat the first week as setup rather than counting it toward adoption metrics.
- Include the optional pre-commit hook in the pilot scope.

## Action items
- [ ] Send the SOC 2 Type I report and penetration test summary today (me).
- [ ] Check with compliance about obtaining an auditor bridge letter and follow up by Thursday (me).
- [ ] Confirm whether Enterprise on-prem scoping is worth pursuing alongside the security review (me).
- [ ] Place a tentative hold on the seventh for pilot kickoff (me).
- [ ] Add the pre-commit hook to the pilot setup document (me).
- [ ] Send a quote for 39 active seats on Business (me).
- [ ] Seek manager approval for a pilot rate and return with a number before Thursday (me).
- [ ] Send the follow-up email within the next hour (me).
- [ ] Confirm the seventh and the pilot group with the platform lead (Marcus).
- [ ] Take the Type II policy questions to legal and ask whether a bridge letter is acceptable (Marcus).
- [ ] Review the Type I report and penetration test summary with legal (security lead).

## Current workflow and pilot goals
- Harbor Freight Logistics has about 45 engineers across platform, routing, and contractors.
  - Six are contractors; two leave at month-end. I estimated roughly 39 active seats, depending on churn.
- Reviews stall on style, naming, unused imports, and missed error handling rather than substantive logic.
  - Marcus reported a median of about three days to first review, followed by another one or two days of back-and-forth.
- Earlier linters were abandoned because of noise, including roughly 900 warnings on day one.
- Most CI runs on Jenkins, with frequent pipeline timeouts; the mobile driver app team uses some GitHub Actions.
  - Lintly supports both, so CI consolidation is not required to start.
- Proposed success measures were review cycle time, style-related review comments, and developer sentiment.
  - Review cycle time is the VP’s priority; Jenkins and GitHub data could establish a first-week baseline.
- A release freeze in the first week of the month could slow adoption.
  - Marcus thinks it covers production deployments only, but engineers will still be busy.

## Product coverage and security
- Lintly surfaces enforced findings by severity and suppresses existing findings through a baseline scan, showing only new PR issues.
- Business and above support Okta SAML and SCIM, plus audit logs exportable to a SIEM.
  - Okta SSO is non-negotiable for Harbor Freight Logistics.
- Source code is analyzed in memory; only findings metadata is retained.
  - Customer code is not used for model training, as stated in the terms and DPA.
- Lintly obtained SOC 2 Type I in March; the Type II observation window runs through the end of Q3, with a report expected in October.
  - Harbor Freight Logistics’ procurement policy requires Type II for vendors with source-code access.
- On-prem deployment is Enterprise-only and usually takes a few weeks with the solutions team.
  - The security lead said keeping code inside their VPC would probably address much of the concern; rejection of SaaS by legal would be a blocker.
- Secret scanning detects common credential patterns and high-entropy strings.
  - It can block PR merges; local commit blocking requires the pre-commit hook. It complements, rather than replaces, a secrets vault or GitHub push protection.

## Pricing and commercial terms
- Pricing is per active developer seat per month; activity means opening or commenting on a PR within the last 30 days.
- Team costs $22 per seat per month, billed annually, including core rules, Jenkins and GitHub Actions integrations, and standard support.
- Business costs $38 per seat per month and adds custom rule authoring, SSO, and audit logs.
  - The quoted estimate for 45 seats was $1,710 monthly, or about $20,400 annually.
- Enterprise has custom pricing and includes on-prem deployment and a dedicated success manager.
- Marcus requested a paid pilot rate, suggesting half price for the first six weeks to make cost approval easier.
  - No pilot discount was approved during the call.

## Open questions
- Will legal accept Type I plus a bridge letter while Type II is pending, or require Enterprise on-prem deployment?
- What exact success targets will define a successful pilot?
- Will security-only blocking be enabled after the initial warn-only period?
- What are the confirmed six-week pilot dates? The seventh is tentative; the earlier suggested end date did not align with a six-week window.

planning.text:
Q1 feature scope and priorities

We narrowed Q1 to five committed features, with a reduced-scope offline sync as the headline, subject to leadership confirmation. AI summaries remain an experiment rather than a roadmap commitment; whether a pilot gets Q1 engineering time is unresolved.

## Decisions

- Include the template gallery in Q1: internal dogfooding this week, January 20 lazy-loading checkpoint, and an external beta target of end of January.
- Make offline sync the Q1 headline, using last-writer-wins with visible conflict copies rather than full CRDT merging, pending leadership confirmation.
  - Estimate: three to four engineering weeks and about two design weeks. Revisit proper merging in Q2 if the data shows a need.
- Include a minimal permissions fix: one effective-permission display explaining access through folders versus direct sharing.
  - Estimate: two engineering weeks and one design week.
- Include styled PDF export, estimated at one to two engineering weeks.
- Include an iOS quick-capture widget, estimated at two engineering weeks; Android is not included in Q1.
- Keep Notion and Evernote import deferred to Q2.
- Defer enterprise SSO and group mapping to Q2 scoping, with no delivery date committed.
- Use a waitlist test for AI summaries, not a committed Q1 feature.

## Action items

- [ ] Record the Notion and Evernote import deferral and nested-table parsing reason in the roadmap document (me).
- [ ] Confirm the reduced offline-sync scope with leadership and explain why full merging is not included (me).
- [ ] Bring AI summary cost numbers to the next sync (me).
- [ ] Add an explicit requirement to the offline-sync spec that release notes explain possible duplicate notes (me).
- [ ] Block an hour Thursday afternoon to review the template gallery empty state (me).
- [ ] Keep the offline-sync spec moving this week so Aiko can start scoping conflict-copy logic (owner unclear).
- [ ] Prepare the template gallery empty state by Thursday (Sven).
- [ ] Design the effective-permission panel within a week (Sven).

## Template gallery and import

- Aiko confirmed the gallery backend is merged behind a flag and functionally ready for internal dogfooding.
  - Lazy-loading thumbnails remain, estimated at half a day; the beta target depends on completing this by January 20.
- Sven’s gallery design reuses the search card component; the zero-saved-templates empty state is still unfinished.
- Import reliability is the reason for deferral.
  - Evernote’s export format, especially nested tables, risks lost formatting in a partially working importer.

## Offline sync

- The main user need is editing offline and syncing after reconnection, rather than merely reading cached notes.
  - Cached reading is unreliable for notes not opened recently.
  - I cited roughly 40% of last quarter’s sync-related tickets as involving lost edits or old note versions.
- Full text-level CRDT merging would be substantially larger.
  - Estimated at six to eight engineer-weeks for the core, plus three to four weeks for mobile clients: realistically a quarter for two engineers.
  - Sven estimated two weeks for a conflict screen plus about one week of usability testing.
- Conflict copies reduce implementation time but can create confusing duplicate notes, particularly when devices edit titles and different body sections offline.
- Sven outlined three status treatments: a quiet cloud icon, an offline banner, or per-note indicators.
  - Per-note indicators seemed most honest but added visual noise.
  - Sven preferred showing both versions for conflict resolution rather than a generic conflict modal.

## Permissions, PDF export and widget

- Aiko flagged scope creep in permissions work.
  - The current owner/editor/viewer model is confusing when folder and direct permissions overlap.
  - Enterprise requests such as SSO group mapping and audit logs are a much larger project.
- Sales pushback on the enterprise deferral is expected; a delivery date should not be promised before sizing.
- PDF export can reuse the HTML export styling engine; font handling may add time.
- Quick capture and read-only recent-notes widgets are different scopes.
  - Android’s widget API was described as fragile; Sven felt iOS-first would be acceptable if communicated clearly.

## AI summaries

- I favored exploring a pilot because of competitive pressure and an existing model partnership.
  - A basic API-backed summary card might take about three weeks, but evaluation and running costs remain unclear.
- Concerns centered on unproven demand, inference costs, quality on messy notes, and an already full Q1 workload.
  - The five selected features were estimated at roughly ten or eleven engineering weeks across people.
  - A month of cost modeling and a small user test were suggested before committing engineering time.
- Sven supported testing demand with a prototype summary button leading to a waitlist, rather than designing a feature that might quickly be dropped.

## Open questions

- Should an AI summaries pilot receive engineering time in Q1? The disagreement remains open, with a checkpoint at the next sync informed by cost numbers and the waitlist test.
- Which offline-status and conflict-resolution UI should be used for the reduced-scope version?

design_review.text:
Payouts queue migration to Postgres

We reviewed moving settlement retries from Redis to Postgres with SKIP LOCKED, while keeping webhook fanout on Redis short term. The design direction was agreed, with prototype work gated on processor idempotency and Go driver checks, and production approval requiring load-test results.

## Decisions
- Move settlement jobs to Postgres using SKIP LOCKED and polling with backoff.
- Keep webhook fanout on Redis for now; revisit it after the Kafka consumer group issues settle.
- Use a local idempotency table keyed by job ID, storing the processor response, rather than relying solely on the processor’s idempotency window.
- Proceed to a prototype once the processor window and driver questions are answered; require load-test numbers before greenlighting production.

## Action items
- [ ] Pull client error logs for both Redis incident windows and post findings in the design doc by Thursday the 23rd (me).
- [ ] Load-test the local idempotency table by March 28 (me).
- [ ] Update the design doc with the review outcomes and tag owners (me).
- [ ] Write the fanout decision doc by the end of next sprint, March 14 (Greg).
- [ ] Review the pgbouncer pool configuration for session-level features and long-running transaction holds (Ola).
- [ ] Check whether the Go driver uses prepared statements under the proposed pool configuration by the 18th (Ola).
- [ ] Contact the processor account team to confirm the idempotency window (owner unclear).

## Migration motivation and scope
- Redis silently dropped jobs during two incidents last quarter attributed to eviction under memory pressure.
  - The postmortem showed rising `evicted_keys`; Greg raised the possibility of swallowed client OOM errors, so the client-side root cause remains unverified.
- Redis enqueue happens after the Postgres commit, leaving a failure gap that can produce a ghost payout state.
- Postgres and pgbouncer are already operated, avoiding a new stateful system.
- Card processor retries account for ninety-something percent of queue volume; internal webhook fanout is smaller but latency-sensitive.

## Idempotency and throughput
- The proposed worker flow claims a row, marks it in progress, commits, calls the processor outside the transaction, then marks completion in a second transaction.
  - A successful processor call followed by a failed completion commit can cause the job to run again.
- Ola flagged a possible mismatch between the processor’s reported 24-hour idempotency window and retries lasting up to three days.
  - The 24-hour figure comes from a sales deck and is unconfirmed; retries beyond the window risk double charging.
- A local response record would allow replaying the outcome without another processor call.
- Measured peak volume is about 340 payouts per second over the last month.
  - One insert and one update per job would add roughly 700 writes per second at peak, beyond queue traffic; capacity has not yet been tested.

## Latency and pooling
- Current Redis end-to-end p99 is around 40 ms, with sub-millisecond enqueue and effectively immediate dequeue when work is available.
- Proposed polling starts at 50 ms and backs off to 500 ms when the queue is empty.
  - Under load, workers should usually find rows immediately; estimated p99 is perhaps 120 ms, but confidence is low.
- LISTEN/NOTIFY is problematic through pgbouncer transaction pooling because a persistent LISTEN connection cannot be held.
- Transaction pooling should suit short claim transactions, but session-level advisory locks and cached prepared statements may cause problems.
  - I think the Go driver may use prepared statements by default and that simple protocol may be configured, but neither was confirmed.
- Keeping Redis for fanout retains two systems operationally.
  - Kafka was floated as a later option, but ledger migration work is ongoing and consumer lag alerts are noisy.

## Rollback and reconciliation
- The proposed rollout uses one week of dual-write, enqueueing to both systems while consuming from only one; rollback would flip the consumer.
  - Fatima raised concerns about draining in-flight Postgres jobs and divergence causing duplicate or missing execution.
- Priya’s team owns the existing nightly reconciler, which compares by job ID.
  - It is currently built for the ledger, not the queue; queue reconciliation remains a gap.

## Open questions
- How will dual-write divergence and in-flight jobs be handled safely during rollback, given that queue reconciliation is not yet built?

brainstorm.text:
Booking app names and positioning

We brainstormed names and positioning for the climbing booking app without choosing a final name. Topout, Slab and Rackly emerged as the main candidates, with trademark checks and another discussion planned for Thursday.

## Decisions
- Keep Beta and Cragline parked while focusing on Topout, Slab and Rackly.
- Retain Belay as a possible feature or brand term rather than a product-name candidate.
- Reconvene Thursday after sleeping on the ideas.

## Action items
- [ ] Run trademark searches for Topout and Slab tonight and send the results around (me).
- [ ] Try taglines that do not lead with failure, ahead of Thursday’s discussion (owner unclear).
- [ ] Ask Dani’s mom about Beta again (Dani).

## Positioning and audiences
- I framed the problem as access: climbers do not know when walls or spots are available around route-setting schedules, so they show up and get turned away.
- The strongest proposed promise was “you’ll actually get on the wall”; booking is the mechanism rather than the benefit.
- The name needs to work for paying gym owners and climbers who download and use the app.
  - Gym owners sign the contracts, while climbers drive brand affinity and word of mouth.
- A neutral name with a climbing-specific tagline could serve both audiences.
  - The counterargument was that a niche product may need to signal climbing immediately.
- Climbing jargon could work in feature names without putting that burden on the main name.
  - Suggestions included “Belay alerts” and “belay queue.”

## Name candidates
- Topout conveys finishing a climb and has the product promise built in.
  - There may already be a gym-management company with that name; someone also thought it sounded like a sports drink.
- Slab is short, one syllable and connected to climbing walls.
  - I worried it could sound like a flooring company or bakery.
- Rackly felt friendly to me, and Tomás liked it.
  - Another reaction was that it sounded like a boat-rental business.
- Beta has both climbing and startup meanings.
  - The software-test meaning could overshadow the climbing meaning; Dani’s mom was raised as a useful outside-the-niche test case.
- Cragline evokes a cliff, route or route map.
  - It also sounded like an airline, prompting concern about transport associations.
- Belay suggests trust and having someone’s back.
  - Pronunciation uncertainty made it a probably unsuitable product name.
- Other suggestions included Route, Crimp, a chalk-based name, Gripfeed and Lead.
  - Holdless was withdrawn; Wallmate was disliked.
  - Access and Gear were considered too generic; Kit too vague and already common.
  - Crux, Send, Basecamp and Clip were seen as taken or crowded. Climbin and Onwall drew negative reactions.

## Tagline ideas
- “Never get turned away at the door” felt strong but led with the failure state.
- “Book your wall” drew a negative reaction and a hotel-ad comparison.
- “You’ll get on the wall” resonated as a more benefit-focused line.

## Open questions
- Which main candidate best balances the access promise, climbing relevance and appeal to both audiences?
- Should the product name explicitly signal climbing, or leave that work to a tagline?
- What tagline best expresses getting on the wall without leading with failure?

customer_support.text:
Northeast field sync failure escalation

We reproduced a sync failure affecting Marcus’s northeast field team and successfully tested a temporary workaround once. I’ll escalate the issue to the sync team and the requested invoice credit to billing today; neither a fix date nor a credit was promised.

## Action items
- [ ] Escalate the sync failure to the sync team today, including reproduction steps, the affected region, and the version rollout timeline (me)
- [ ] Send Marcus written instructions for the temporary workaround (me)
- [ ] Send billing the escalation today with the reported $9,000–$11,000 in re-dispatch labor costs, the 41-of-163 job report, reproduction steps, and app/OS versions; copy Marcus and ask billing to respond directly (me)

## Sync failure and reproduction
- Marcus reported almost two weeks of disrupted field syncing, with 41 of 163 jobs incomplete on the server in the report pulled Thursday.
  - Reinstalling twice and completely wiping one phone did not resolve the issue.
- Devices are running app version 4.11.3 on iOS eighteen point two.
  - The build rolled out to the organization on the eighth; Marcus thinks the first complaints arrived around the tenth and says the issue has worsened.
- Offline jobs appear complete on the phone, but dashboard data is missing or partial.
  - Checklists sometimes arrive without photos; Dev Patel also reported photos arriving while the job record remains “pending sync.”
- Dev reproduced the failure by creating an offline job with a checklist, two photos, and a signature, then reconnecting.
  - The device briefly showed syncing, then “synced,” but Marcus could not find “test one” on the dashboard.
  - Dev confirmed the photos were attached to the job on the device.
- The reproduction suggests a gap between local data capture and server receipt or handling; root cause remains unconfirmed.

## Temporary workaround
- Keeping the app in the foreground for about 30 seconds after reconnecting, then manually syncing from the job menu, worked for “test two.”
  - The job and photos appeared on the web dashboard.
  - This has reduced failures for some other teams on this build, but one successful test is not proof of reliability.
- I recommended testing a few more jobs over the next day before relying on the workaround.
- Marcus objected to technicians having to babysit their phones and emphasized that this is not a fix.
- I advised replying directly to the email thread and flagging a regression if the workaround stops working or new failures occur.

## Business impact and credit request
- Marcus said technicians cannot close out jobs and have had to return to sites to redo completed work.
  - He estimated $9,000–$11,000 in re-dispatch labor costs over the last two weeks.
- Contract renewal is three weeks away, and Marcus is under pressure from his VP.
- Marcus requested a credit on the current invoice, not a discount on next year’s contract.
  - Billing must decide whether to approve a credit and the amount; I cannot authorize it.

## Open questions
- What is causing the sync failure, and when can engineering deliver a fix?
- Will the workaround remain reliable across additional jobs?
- Will billing approve the requested current-invoice credit, and for how much?

offsite_logistics.text:
Porto offsite planning and logistics

We chose Porto for the 12-person offsite and confirmed a €1,200-per-person budget, with flights reimbursed separately. Planning responsibilities are assigned, but the stated March 9–11 dates need clarification against the Sunday-arrival, Wednesday-departure schedule.

## Decisions
- Hold the offsite in Porto, at the shortlisted converted warehouse venue in Ribeira.
- Budget €1,200 per person for hotel, food, the venue room and the activity; reimburse flights separately.
- Use name badges, since new hire Kenji is attending.
- Meet again Thursday.

## Action items
- [ ] Find two or three tile-painting and wine-tour options, with pricing and availability, by next Friday (me).
- [ ] Draft the offsite agenda (me).
- [ ] Handle the travel document, including airport transfers (Dana).
- [ ] Arrange the hotel block with the courtyard hotel and confirm the room count (owner unclear).
- [ ] Confirm the 20% hotel deposit amount by Wednesday and arrange the deposit by the end of the month (owner unclear).
- [ ] Handle name badges and printing (owner unclear).
- [ ] Send meeting notes, including to Dana, who joined at the end (owner unclear).

## Venue and travel
- Lisbon’s venue near Alfama was €1,400 more expensive overall.
- Porto offers shorter flights for most of the team; Lisbon adds a connection for half the people in Denver.

## Dates and schedule
- March 9–11 was repeated as the date range, but March 9 was checked and confirmed to be Sunday.
- The discussed schedule was Sunday arrival, sessions Monday March 10 and Tuesday March 11, then a Wednesday half-day and departure.
  - Three nights were agreed, which does not align with the stated March 9–11 range.

## Activities and logistics
- Tile painting and a wine tour remain the activity options under consideration.
  - Surf lessons cost about €90 per person and could leave non-surfers uncomfortable.
  - Tile painting was favored as a distinctly Porto activity.
- The courtyard hotel has already been emailed; the deposit will be 20%.
- Marcus withdrew from badges and printing because he will be attending a conference that week.
- A draft agenda is needed to avoid the lack of structure at the previous offsite.

## Open questions
- What is the final date range: March 9–11, or Sunday March 9 through Wednesday departure?
- Which activity will be selected after pricing and availability are reviewed?

numbers.text:
Q3 financial review and renewals

We reviewed Q3 actuals, hiring costs and upcoming vendor renewals for the board pack. We agreed on how to present the unresolved storage costs and cash timing, narrowed the backfill searches, and identified checks needed before finalizing the figures.

## Decisions
- Describe the storage overage as “under review” in the variance memo without committing to a number until Priya has checked it.
- Footnote the agreed extension of vendor payables in the cash figures.
- Close the finance analyst and second support lead backfill searches; keep the other three open.
- Use $2.97 million as the monthly payroll planning figure at full headcount, rounded to $3.0 million in the deck.

## Action items
- [ ] Review expense-tool usage and seat requirements with the team at the January review (me).
- [ ] Check the HR system to confirm the approved headcount plan is 228 and, if 230 is a stale draft, send Hannah the correction today (me).
